gendered_labor.assessment: Labor divided by sex (men: farming, hunting, crafts; women: trading, food processing, mat-weaving, pottery, cooking) but with documented situational flexibility, not rigidity; women held a dominant, well-evidenced role in long-distance trade specifically, a major avenue for wealth accumulation and title-acquisition.

sources.citation: General ethnographic/historical consensus on Yorùbá gendered labor and women's trade dominance.

political_inequality.assessment: Central state offices (Aláàfin, Òyó Mèsì, most town obas) were predominantly male, but the Ìyálóde title ("mother of the women") held real, non-ceremonial legislative and judicial authority on councils alongside male chiefs; a named historical example, Efúnṣetán Aníwúrà (second Ìyálóde of Ìbàdàn), built one of the largest 19th-century fortunes via long-distance trade (including the slave trade) and used wealth/position to strengthen Ìbàdàn's military. Does NOT demonstrate comparable rates of office-holding between men and women, nor integration into the general chieftaincy structure beyond the parallel women's-affairs office.

sources.citation: Bolanle Awe, doctoral work on 19th-century militarized Ìbàdàn (pioneering Nigerian historian of women); general secondary sourcing on the Ìyálóde/Ìyálója/Ìyálàje titles and Efúnṣetán Aníwúrà.

legal_economic_status.assessment: Both men and women held rights to possess property including land, generally as communal/family rather than strictly individual property in the precolonial era. Multiple sources frame colonial administration as having fixed binary gender categories and concentrated property/inheritance rights in male hands via imposed patrilineal succession rules — an increase in gender-based property restriction attributed to the colonial period, not a straightforward codification of a preexisting patriarchal baseline. This causal claim could not be traced to one specific peer-reviewed citation with a named author in this research pass.

sources.citation: General literature associated with the Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí school on colonial-era gender-category imposition.

household_authority.assessment: Insa Nolte, "Yoruba Histories of Marriage and Belonging: Gender, Power and Innovation in Eighteenth-Century West Africa," Gender & History (Wiley), using ìtàn (oral-historical genre) as evidence, argues marriage structured 18th-century Yorùbá political/social change and that patrilineal kinship associated "husbandly" authority-and-belonging-by-birth roles with power, and "wifely" support/outsider-origin roles with less — but crucially "husbandly roles were frequently open to women," i.e. authority attached more to a kinship role than to biological sex per se.

sources.citation: Nolte, Insa. "Yoruba Histories of Marriage and Belonging: Gender, Power and Innovation in Eighteenth-Century West Africa." Gender & History, Wiley.

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: Polygyny was normative/legal for men (multiple wives); no source found showing an equivalent legal/customary allowance for women to take multiple husbands — an asymmetry, though thinly sourced beyond this. Premarital chastity norms, adultery penalties by sex, and divorce-initiation rights specifically for precolonial Yorùbá society were not confirmed by academic sourcing in this research pass.

sources.citation: General ethnographic consensus on normative Yorùbá polygyny.

ideological_patriarchy.assessment: DISPUTED at the center of Yorùbá gender scholarship. Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí, The Invention of Women: Making an African Sense of Western Gender Discourses (University of Minnesota Press, 1997), argues gender was not an indigenous organizing principle in precolonial Yorùbá society — social hierarchy ran on seniority (age), not sex, and systematic gender categorization/ideological subordination was a colonial import. Bibi Bakare-Yusuf, "Yorubas Don't Do Gender: A Critical Review of Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí's The Invention of Women," directly challenges this as overstated. No independent third source citing specific Yorùbá proverbs/oral literature/ritual texts asserting female natural subordination was located — the dispute itself is documented; the underlying primary textual evidence is thin on both sides.

sources.citation: Oyěwùmí, Oyèrónkẹ́. The Invention of Women: Making an African Sense of Western Gender Discourses. University of Minnesota Press, 1997.
sources.author: Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí

sources.citation: Bakare-Yusuf, Bibi. "Yorubas Don't Do Gender: A Critical Review of Oyèrónkẹ́ Oyěwùmí's The Invention of Women."
sources.author: Bibi Bakare-Yusuf

dimensions.notes: Ifá priesthood (babaláwo) gender: historically male-dominated in most documented lineages; the Iyanifa/Ìyánífá controversy over female initiation is live and explicitly split by lineage (Nigerian lineages more accepting; some Cuban Lucumí lineages rejecting) — see claim_iyanifa_controversy. Required does_not_demonstrate note: Efúnṣetán Aníwúrà and the Ìyálóde institution demonstrate some Yorùbá women held real political/economic power; they do NOT demonstrate general gender egalitarianism or resolve the Oyěwùmí/Bakare-Yusuf dispute.
